          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. This Court vide order dated 13.04.2026 requested the learned
Amicus  Curiae  to prepare an online and accessible questionnaire,
seeking details of all the IAs pending in the instant Writ
Petition(s). The information sought through the questionnaire was
also illustrated in Paragraph 19 of the said order. The concerned
AOR or the Party-in-Person, who have filed the IAs were asked to
fill the online questionnaire on or before 15.06.2026. It was made
clear, in Paragraph 22 of the said order, that if the AOR or the
Party-in-Person failed to furnish the requisite information, it
shall be presumed that their respective IAs have been rendered
infructuous and shall stand dismissed accordingly.
2. In deference thereto, learned  Amicus  has filed a note for
hearing on the categorization of the pending IAs and a format
(Appendix A) has been appended containing the questionnaire. The
16

--- Page 61 ---
said format has already been circulated amongst the AORs and the
Party-in-Person(s). It is disclosed that, as on 21.09.2026, 90
responses have been received from the concerned AORs. As such, it
has been submitted that the remaining IAs are liable to be
dismissed as infructuous in view of Paragraph 22 of our order dated
13.04.2026.
3. The learned Amicus  has further appended a list (Appendix B)
where the concerned AORs have informed that these IAs have become
infructuous. Owing to this, all the IAs mentioned in Appendix B,
i.e., I.A. No.2702 of 2008, I.A. Nos.125603-125604 of 2025, I.A.
No.925/2003 [in Contempt Petition (Civil) No.193 of 2001 in W.P.(C)
No.202 of 1995], I.A. Diary No. 104052 of 2023, I.A. No.306241 of
2025, and I.A. No.306242 of 2025 are hereby disposed of as having
become infructuous.
4. Learned Amicus  has on the basis of the information gathered
from the AORs categorized the remaining pending IAs as per Appendix
C. It may be seen from Clause 14 of the format in Appendix A that
there are nine categories for classification of the pending IAs.
With a view to provide a final opportunity, we deem it appropriate
to direct that all applications in respect of which no response has
been received from the AORs so far (except contempt petitions) be
listed before the Registrar’s Court to give one more opportunity to
the AORs to fill up the format (Appendix A) and submit the same in
respect of their pending IAs. Such opportunity shall be granted to
them for a period of one week only. Thereafter, other IAs, in which
no response has been elicited, will be deemed to be dismissed for
non-prosecution.  Additionally,  the  AORs  may  submit  their
17

--- Page 62 ---
objection(s), if any, to the categorization of their pending IAs by
the learned Amicus. 
5. All the IAs mentioned in Appendix C are ordered to be listed
category-wise, after taking directions on the administrative side
from the Chief Justice of India. 
6. Meanwhile,  learned  Amicus  may,  in  consultation  with  Ms.
Aishwarya Bhati, learned Additional Solicitor General of India also

2026 INSC 1042
Civil Appeal No. 6909/2015                                          Page 1 of 10 
 NON-REPORTABLE 
 
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
 
 
CIVIL APPEAL NO. 6909 OF 2015 
 
 
SMT. MANIKA PAUL & ORS. … APPELLANT(S) 
  
VERSUS 
 
THE NEW INDIA ASSURANCE 
CO. LTD. & ORS.                      
 
… RESPONDENT(S) 
 
 
 
O R D E R 
 
1. The present appeal challenges the judgment dated 
05.02.2015 passed by the High Court of Tripura at 
Agartala (hereinafter, "High Court") in MFA (W/C) No. 
17 of 2007. By that judgment, the appeal preferred 
by The New India Assurance Co. Ltd., Respondent 
No. 1 herein (hereinafter, "Insurer"), was allowed. The 
judgment/award dated 31.05.2007 passed by the 
Commissioner, Workmen's Compensation, West 
Tripura, Agartala (hereinafter, "Commissioner") in 
T.S. (W/C) No. 48 of 2005, granting compensation of 

--- Page 116 ---
Civil Appeal No. 6909/2015                                          Page 2 of 10 
Rs. 3,22,855/- with interest to the Appellants, was 
thereby set aside. 
 
2. I.A. No. 32034 of 2022 has been filed seeking deletion 
of Appellant No. 3, Shri Suresh Paul (also known as 
Suresh Chandra Paul), the father of the deceased. He 
expired on 02.11.2020 during the pendency of the 
present appeal. The mother of the deceased is already 
on record as Appellant No. 4. The application is 
allowed, and the name of Appellant No. 3 stands 
deleted from the array of parties. 
 
3. Briefly, the facts are as follows. Suman Paul 
(hereinafter, "deceased"), aged about 28 years, was 
engaged as a driver of a Santro Zing car bearing 
registration No. TR -01-H-0792. The car was owned 
by one Babul Dey (since deceased) and insured with 
the Insurer. On 17.11.2004, at  about 5:00 to 5:30 
p.m., the deceased was called by the owner and, on 
his instructions, drove the officials of Nicholas 
Piramal company, who were staying at Rajdhani 
Hotel, Agartala. The deceased did not return home 
that night. His wife, Appellant No. 1, kept calling the 
house of the owner from about 1:00 a.m. At about 

--- Page 117 ---
Civil Appeal No. 6909/2015                                          Page 3 of 10 
3:30 a.m. the wife of the owner informed her that the 
deceased had left the car in the garage at about 9:30 
p.m. and gone away. A missing report was lodged on 
18.11.2004. On 21.11.2004, his dead body was 
found in a drain near the Women's College Hostel, 
about 150 metres from Rajdhani Hotel. West Agartala 
P.S. Case No. 145 of 2004 under Section 302 of the 
Indian Penal Code, 1860 was registered on the report 
of his father. 
 
4. The case of the Appellants before the Commissioner 
was that an entertainment programme  had 
continued at Rajdhani Hotel till midnight, and that 
the deceased was waiting with the car outside the 
hotel, where Gunen Chandra Deb (PW-2) saw him at 
about 10:30 to 10:50 p.m. The owner, examined as 
DW-1, deposed that the officials returned to the hotel 
at about 8:45 to 9:00 p.m. According to him, the 
deceased then brought the car back, parked it in the 
garage at about 9:15 to 9:30 p.m., and handed over 
the keys to his wife, the owner himself being away 
from the house at the time. The Commissioner 
believed PW-2 and drew an adverse inference from 
the non -examination of the owner's wife. He also 

--- Page 118 ---
Civil Appeal No. 6909/2015                                          Page 4 of 10 
relied upon the First Information Report and the 
seizure of the car during investigation. On that basis, 
he held that it "can be safely presumed" that the 
deceased was murdered in the course of his 
employment, and  awarded compensation of Rs. 
3,22,855/- with interest at 12% per annum. 
 
5. The High Court did not accept the stand of the owner 
that the deceased was not his employee. It, however, 
disbelieved PW-2. His name was not disclosed in the 
claim petition. Though he claimed to know the family 
for about fifteen years, he informed neither the family 
nor the police during the four days the d eceased 
remained untraced. He admitted that Rajdhani Hotel 
did not fall on the shortest route to his house. And 
his statement had not been recorded by the police. 
The High Court further noticed that no suggestion 
was put to DW -1 in cross -examination that t he car 
was not parked in the garage at 9:30 p.m. It 
concluded that the employment of the deceased for 
the day had come to an end once he parked the car 
and left, that the murder took place later in the night 
for reasons not known, and that the Appellants h ad 
failed to discharge the burden of establishing a 

--- Page 119 ---
Civil Appeal No. 6909/2015                                          Page 5 of 10 
causal connection between the death and the 
employment. 
 
6. Learned counsel for the Appellants has asserted that 
the finding regarding the car having been parked at 
9:30 p.m. rests on hearsay. The wife of the owner, 
who is said to have received the keys, was never 
examined, and DW -1 himself admitted that he did 
not meet the deceased after 5:30 p.m. The further 
submission is that PW -2 is an independent witness 
whose testimony was rightly accepted by the 
Commissioner. The First Information Report records 
that the deceased had been working as the owner's 
driver for about four months, and the seizure of the 
car shows that the deceased was engaged with the 
vehicle at the time of his death. It is also urged that 
the High Court failed to apply the doctrine of notional 
extension. On these assertions, the judgment of the 
High Court is sought to be assailed. 
 
7. On the other hand, the Insurer has supported the 
impugned judgment. It submits that the deceased 
parked the car in the garage at 9:30 p.m., handed 
over the keys and left, whereupon his employment 

--- Page 120 ---
Civil Appeal No. 6909/2015                                          Page 6 of 10 
came to an end. The version of his presence at 
Rajdhani Hotel was disbelieved on appreciation of 
evidence, and the murder has no causal connection 
with the employment. On this basis, it is submitted 
that the impugned judgment does not call for any 
interference. 
 
8. We have considered the submissions and perused the 
record. Under Section 3(1) of the Workmen's 
Compensation Act, 1923 (hereinafter, "Act"), the 
employer is liable where personal injury is caused to 
a workman "by accident arising out of and in the 
course of his employment". Both requirements must 
be satisfied, and the onus is upon the claimant. This 
Court in Mackinnon Mackenzie & Co. Private Ltd. 
v. Ibrahim Mohammad Issak , 1969 ACJ 419 has  
held as follows: 
"Although the onus of proving that the 
injury by accident arose both out of and in 
the course of employment rests upon the 
applicant these essentials may be inferred 
when the facts proved justify the 
inference. On the one hand the 
Commissioner must not sur mise, 
conjecture or guess; on the other hand, he 
may draw an inference from the proved 
facts so long as it is a legitimate 
inference.” 
 

--- Page 121 ---
Civil Appeal No. 6909/2015                                          Page 7 of 10 
9. The employment of the deceased with the owner has 
been accepted by the High Court and is not in issue 
before us. What, therefore, is required to be seen is 
whether the deceased was on duty when he met his 
death. There is no direct evidence on this aspect. The 
circumstances in which, and the reasons for which, 
the deceased was murdered have remained 
unknown. 
 
10. What is significant to note is that the version of the 
car having been parked in the garage at 9:30 p.m. is 
not merely a statement of DW -1 rather i t is the 
information which the family of the deceased itself 
received from the owner's wife that very night. The 
father of the deceased recorded it in the First 
Information Report, the Appellants pleaded it in the 
claim petition, and Appellant No. 1 (PW-1) reiterated 
it in her affidavit. In her cross -examination, PW -1 
stated that she could not say whether her husband 
had been relieved from duty at 9:30 p.m. after 
keeping the vehicle in the garage of the owner. DW-1 
was not confronted with any suggestion to the 
contrary. In this light, the non -examination of the 

--- Page 122 ---
Civil Appeal No. 6909/2015                                          Page 8 of 10 
owner's wife is of no consequence, and the plea of 
hearsay does not merit acceptance. 
 
11. The only evidence against this version is that of PW -
2. The reasons assigned by the High Court for not 
relying upon him are based on the record, and largely 
on his own admissions in cross-examination. We find 
no perversity in the said appreciation. The finding of 
the Commissioner, on the other hand, rested on a 
presumption rather than on an inference legitimately 
drawn from proved facts, which is precisely what 
Ibrahim Mohammad Issak (supra) cautions 
against. 
 
12. The other circumstances pressed by the Appellants 
do not advance their case. The fact that the deceased 
had worked with the owner for some months 
establishes the employment, which is a finding not in 
dispute. The seizure of the car of the owner in the 
investigation of the murder of its driver, by itself, does 
not indicate that the deceased was with the vehicle, 
or was attacked while driving or guarding it, when he 
was killed. The recovery of the dead body about 150 
metres from the hotel only shows proximity to the 

--- Page 123 ---
Civil Appeal No. 6909/2015                                          Page 9 of 10 
place, not a connection with the employment. It 
cannot supply the basic fact that the workman was 
engaged in, or in connection with, his employment 
when the fatal injury was sustained. The doctrine of 
notional extension, as explained in General 
Manager, B.E.S.T. Undertaking, Bombay v. 
Agnes, AIR 1964 SC 193 , on which reliance is 
sought to be placed by the appellants depends on the 
circumstances of each case.  The decisions relied 
upon by the Appellants were cases where the 
workman was, at the relevant time, with the vehicle 
or on an errand of the employer. That is not so in the 
present case. 
 
13. We are, thus, in agreement with the view taken by the 
High Court that the Appellants have failed to 
discharge the burden cast upon them under Section 
3(1) of the Act. The view taken is a plausible one on 
the evidence on record, and does not call for any 
interference. 
 
14. In view of the above, I.A. No. 32034 of 2022 stands 
allowed in the terms indicated in paragraph 2. The 
present appeal is dismissed, and the judgment dated 

--- Page 124 ---
Civil Appeal No. 6909/2015                                          Page 10 of 10 
05.02.2015 passed by the High Court in MFA (W/C) 
No. 17 of 2007 is upheld. The interim order dated 
03.07.2015 stands vacated. Any amount paid to, or 
withdrawn by, the Appellants under the award dated 
31.05.2007 passed by the Commissioner in T.S. 
(W/C) No. 48 of 2005 shall not be recovered from 
them. No order as to costs. 
 
15. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

separate orders dated 25.03.2026 passed
in S.B. Criminal Misc. Bail Application
Nos. 15618/2025, 4367/2026 and 4400/2026.
3. He sought the relief of bail in relation
to First Information Report (FIR)  No.
233/2025 dated 27.06.2025 registered with
Police  Station  –  Kalwar,  District  –
Jaipur West, Rajasthan, for the offences
                      1

--- Page 143 ---
punishable under Sections 318(4), 316(2),
316(5), 329(3) and 61(2) of the Bharatiya
Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 1. He was arrested in
connection with this FIR on 03.10.2025.
4. He also sought bail in connection with
FIR  No.  361 /2025  dated  17.10.2025
registered with the same Police Station
for  the  offences  punishable  under
Sections  318(4),  316(5),  338,  340(2),
61(2)(b)  and 336(2)  of  the  BNS ,  in
relation to which he was arrested on
06.02.2026.
5. Lastly, he also sought bail in relation
to FIR No. 382/2025 dated  12.11.2025,
registered with the same Police Station,
for  the  offences  punishable  under
Sections 318(4), 316(2), 338, 61(2)(b),
336(2), 336(3) and 340(2) of the BNS , in
connection with which, he was arrested on
29.01.2026.
6. We are informed that chargesheets have
been filed in relation to the aforestated
three FIRs. However, the learned counsel
appearing  for  the  State  of  Rajasthan
1 “BNS”, for short
                      2

--- Page 144 ---
asserts that the investigation is still
pending in relation to certain documents
and also against other accused.

since  03.10.2025  and  the  chargesheets
have already been filed in relation to
the  aforestated  FIRs,  we  are  of  the

“1) There  was  an  old  building

1. We are informed by the learned counsel for the parties
that pursuant to the Mediation, t he parties have amicably

2. The Settlement Agreement dated 04.08.2026 between the
parties, is in the following terms:-
“5. Both the parties hereto have arrived at an amicable
settlement on the following terms and conditions for
dissolution of marriage by mutual consent:-
A. Custody  of  the  minor  child  Anayara  shall
remain with the respondent-wife.
B. Visitation  Right:-  Petitioner  No.3-Husband
will meet the child once in a month as agreed
between the parties preferably on a Sunday for
maximum period of 3-5 hours. The petitioner
No.3-Husband will meet the child Anayara in
presence of respondent-wife or her Maternal
Grand Parents;
1

--- Page 164 ---
C. That  the  parties  have  agreed  that  the
petitioner  No.3-Husband  will  pay  to  the
Respondent-wife a total sum of Rs.12,00,000/-
(Rupees Twelve Lakhs only) towards full and
final settlement of all her claims towards her
permanent  alimony,  stridhan,  maintenance
(past,  present,  future)  alongwith  the
maintenance of the child and any other claim
whatsoever;
D. That the petitioner No.3 Husband shall make
the payment with a period of 2 months from the
date of signing this agreement i.e. on or
before 4.10.2026;
E. It is jointly agreed between the parties that
they  will  move  an  application  before  the
Hon’ble Supreme Court under Article 142 of the
Constitution of India for invoking inherent
powers of the Hon’ble Supreme Court praying
for  divorce  by  mutual  consent  and
withdrawal/quashing  of  any  or  all  pending
cases  between  the  parties  as  parties  are
staying separately since 26.04.2024 i.e. for
the last more than two years and there is
irretrievable break down of the marriage.
6. That the Petitioners or their relatives and the
Respondent or her relatives have agreed that none of
them will initiate any other legal action, Civil Suit
or complaint against each other or against the family
members of each other in respect of their matrimonial
dispute in future.
7. That subject to the aforesaid terms, the parties
have resolved all the disputes amicably in relation to
the marriage and have been left with no claims against
2

--- Page 165 ---
each other or their respective family members.
8.  That by signing this Agreement the parties hereto
solemnly state and affirm that they have no further
claims  or  demands  against  each  other  including
maintenance, or any movable or immovable property and
all the disputes and differences have been amicably
settled by the parties hereto through the process of
mediation.

conditions set out in the above mentioned Settlement
Agreement, which have been arrived with free will of
the parties without any coercion, duress or collusion
and  parties  undertake  not  to  raise  any  dispute
whatsoever henceforth.

all her claims. The respondent-wife acknowledged the receipt

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.       OF 2026
(ARISING OUT OF S.L.P. (C) NO. 24351 OF 2026)
RAJESH NOLKHA & ORS. ...APPELLANTS
VERSUS
RANI TIBRAWALLA & ANR.     ...RESPONDENTS
O R D E R
1. Leave granted. 
2. In the present case, the respondents/plaintiffs, on
03rd January, 2022, filed Title Suit No.05 of 2022 on the file
of the City Civil Court at Calcutta, inter  alia,  seeking
recovery of the Khas possession of the suit premises from
the appellants.  Prayers for mesne profit and consequential
reliefs were also made.  
3. On 19th May, 2022, the appellants entered appearance
through their Advocate and filed vakalatnama and written
statement. On 21st January, 2023, the written statement was
directed to be accepted and the suit was posted for framing
of the issues on 08 th June, 2023.  On 08 th June, 2023,
issues were framed and the suit was fixed for peremptory
hearing on 05 th September, 2023.  On 05 th September, 2023,
the  appellants,  in  spite  of  repeated  calls,  remained
absent.  The learned trial Court directed the suit to be
1

--- Page 177 ---
proceeded with ex-parte.  Thereafter, after recording the
ex-parte evidence of the respondents, on 17th October, 2023,
decreed the suit and directed the appellants to deliver
vacant possession within three months.
4. Claiming that on 08 th August, 2024, they received
information  of  the  suit  being  decreed  ex-parte  and
contending that the clerk missed noting the date of 05 th
September, 2023, when the Court posted the suit for 05 th
September, 2023 vide  order dated 08 th June, 2023. On the
application for setting aside the ex-parte  decree with an
appropriate application seeking condonation of delay of 273
days was filed on 17th August, 2024.  
5. On 14th July, 2025, the learned trial Court dismissed
the application for condonation of delay, holding that the
explanation  tendered  was  not  sufficient.  An  appeal  was
preferred  before  the  High  Court  at  Calcutta  by  the
appellants.  The High Court, vide impugned order dated 22nd
June, 2026, after condoning the delay of 75 days in filing
the appeal, confirmed the order of the trial Court refusing
to condone delay in filing the application under Order IX
Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (for short,
‘CPC’).  Aggrieved, the appellants are before us.
6. We have heard Mr. Sahib Singh Sohel, learned counsel
2

--- Page 178 ---
appearing for the appellants and Mr. Rohit Amit Sthalekar,
learned counsel appearing for the contesting respondents
and also perused the records.
7. The learned counsel for the appellants submits that
it was an inadvertent error on the part of the Advocate’s
clerk, which resulted in the date of 05 th September, 2023
being missed, resulting in the consequential orders of
eviction.  The learned counsel prays that one opportunity
to defend the suit be provided for.  The learned counsel
undertakes that no further adjournments will be sought for
and a time bound direction be issued for disposal of the
suit. The learned counsel also submits that the parties may
be put to terms. 
8. The learned counsel appearing for the respondents
vehemently opposes the contention of the appellants.  The
learned  counsel  contends  that  at  every  stage,  the
appellants have attempted to delay the progress of the
suit.  The learned counsel also contends that on merits,
the appellants have no case since they are unauthorised
occupants.   According  to  the  respondents,  under  the
Statute,  post the death of the original tenant, the spouse
can claim occupancy right for the life time and the
appellants who are sons and daughter, have no right. 
3

--- Page 179 ---
9. Be that as it may.  Those are the matters to be
decided on merits.  
10. Having considered the matter, we are of the opinion
that one opportunity may be given to the appellants to
defend the suit and the orders of the trial Court and the
High Court deserve to be set aside. 
11. Hence, the order of the trial Court dated 14 th July,
2023 and the order of the High Court dated 22 nd June, 2026,
stand set aside. 
12. We condone the delay in filing the application under
Order IX Rule 13 of the CPC and consequently, set aside the
ex-parte decree dated 17th October, 2023 and remit the Title
Suit No. 05 of 2022 to the City Civil Court, Calcutta for
disposal, from the stage of recording of evidence of the
respondents/plaintiffs.
13. Considering that there has been delay caused at the
behest of the appellants, we direct that the appellants
shall pay a sum of Rs.50,000/- as cost to the respondents
within a period of four weeks from today.  We, further,
direct  that  since  the  delay  has  been  caused  by  the
appellants, the suit itself should be disposed of within a
period of six months from today.  The trial Court, for the
purpose  of  recording  of  evidence,  shall  grant  two
4

--- Page 180 ---
opportunities to each party for concluding the evidence and
dispose of the entire suit on or before 28th February, 2027.
14. The learned counsel appearing for the respondents
submits that pursuant to the order of this Court dated 31 st
August, 2026, the respondents have received a sum of
Rs.1,02,320/- from the appellants. 
15. We make it clear that the said amount is without
prejudice to the rights and contentions of the appellants
and will be subject to the outcome of the suit. 
16. Parties are directed to appear before City Civil
Court, Calcutta on 28th September, 2026.
17. Accordingly, the appeal stands disposed of in the
above terms. 
18. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO. 3713 of 2023
UNITED INDIA INSURANCE COMPANY LTD ..... APPELLANT
                  VERSUS
M/S. GVR COLD STORAGE ..... RESPONDENT
O R D E R
1. United  India  Insurance  Company  Ltd.,  the  appellant,  is
aggrieved by the order dated 04.01.2023 passed by the National
Consumer  Disputes  Redressal  Commission 1,  New  Delhi,  in
Consumer Case No. 54 of 2014. By the said order, the NCDRC
directed  the  appellant  to  pay  to  the  respondent,  the
complainant in Consumer Case No. 54 of 2014, a sum of
3,34,25,044/- (Rupees three crore thirty four lakh twenty₹
five thousand forty four only) along with interest. 
2. The complainant in Consumer Case No. 54/2014, the respondent
herein, secured two standard fire and special perils insurance
polices from the appellant for its buildings, machinery, cold
storage equipment and the stock in the cold storage. 
3. These polices covered the period from 09.08.2010 to 18.08.2011
and 06.05.2011 to 05.09.2011 respectively. While so, it was
the case of the respondent, that on the evening of 06.07.2011,
owing to torrential rains, a chamber of the cold storage plant
1  For short ‘NCDRC’
1

--- Page 183 ---
collapsed, causing damage to the building as well as the stock
stored therein. On this basis,  claims wer e raised by the
respondent  against  the  appellant  in  January,  2012.  The
appellant appointed a licensed surveyor in relation thereto.
Basing  on  the  surveyor’s  report  dated  05.02.2012,  the
appellant repudiated the claim of the respondent by letter
dated 27.02.2012.
4. As the appellant did not act upon the respondent’s legal
notice dated 27.03.2012, calling upon it to pay the insurance
claims, the respondent approach the NCDRC by of way the
subject consumer case.
5. We may note that the Manager of the respondent addressed
letter dated 29.07.2011 to the appellant.  Therein, he stated
that owing to the thunder and rain, Chamber-B and the R.C.C.
slab had collapsed. 
6. The Final Survey Report dated 05.02.2012 submitted by Rank
Surveyors Pvt. Ltd., an approved surveyor under Section 64UM
of the Insurance Act, 1938 2, assumes great significance in
this regard. Therein, it was noted that the Manager of the
respondent had reported that the collapse had occurred due to
thunder and rain.  During the Surveyor’s inspection onsite,
information relating to the accident was conveyed by the
representatives of the respondent. They also stated to the
effect that there was loud noise/sound followed by heavy dust
and this had taken place due to collapse of the building. 
2  “Act of 1938”, for short
2

--- Page 184 ---
7. Dealing with the cause of loss, the surveyor noted that in the
claim form submitted on 10.01.2012, the cause of the loss was
indicated as unknown. In the initial intimation, however, it
was stated that the loss was due to thunder. No evidence was
produced before the surveyor in support of this cause.  
8. A Senior Civil Engineer was appointed by the surveyor to
analyze the cause of loss and also furnish an assessment of
the loss in respect of the building.  The Senior Civil Engineer
noted in his analysis report that there was a structural
failure and gave full details as to why he opined that the
structure was not in a good condition. He blamed the improper
structural design, poor quality of material and poor quality
of workmanship. He also observed one important point, that is,
that the electric pipes were running inside the columns and
beams with switch controls on the columns. He observed that
the failure of the structure due to this was unavoidable. 
9. The surveyor concluded that the loss caused to the building,
plant and machinery and stock was not due to any of the perils
covered by the insurance policies, that is, fire, lightning,
explosion, implosion, etc., and was squarely attributable to
the structural defects in the building construction. The
surveyor,  accordingly,  reported  that  the  claim  was
inadmissible. Despite the same, the surveyor assessed the
loss, quantifying the same at 52,43,881/- (Rupees fifty two₹
lakh forty three thousand eight hundred eighty one only). 
10. We find that the NCDRC failed to give due weightage to the
3

--- Page 185 ---
surveyor’s report in the context of the structural defects
found in the construction which, according to the surveyor,
were directly responsible for the collapse of the building. 
11. Reliance was only placed upon the self-serving certificates
produced  by  the  respondent  as  to  the  stability  of  the
structure,  which  had  been  obtained  before  the  incident.
Notably, the respondent did not even adduce any evidence in
the context of the specific defects in the construction that
had been pointed out by the Senior Civil Engineer, whose
report was taken into consideration by the surveyor. 
12. Further, we find that the NCDRC did not even undertake any
independent assessment to compute the net loss suffered by the
respondent and granted the sum as claimed by the respondent,
far in excess of the net loss assessed by the approved
surveyor. There is no discussion whatsoever on this aspect and
the NCDRC seems to have blindly accepted the claims put forth
by the respondent without reference to the law laid down by
this Court in United India Insurance Co. Ltd. & Ors. v. Roshan
Lal Oil Mills Ltd. & Ors. 3  Therein, this Court noted that the
NCDRC cannot ignore the report submitted by the approved
surveyor appointed under Section 64UM of the Act of 1938 and
held that non-consideration of such a report would result in
serious miscarriage of justice, vitiating the very order
passed by the NCDRC.  
13. This edict is squarely applicable in the present case as we
3  (2000) 10SCC 19
4

--- Page 186 ---
find that the NCDRC not only ignored the report submitted by
the approved surveyor but blindly accepted the claims put
forth by the respondent in all respects. We find that, in the
consumer case, the respondent claimed that the cause of the
building collapse was lightning. This seems to have been an
afterthought on the part of the respondent, as it was not
projected earlier, either before the appellant or before the
approved surveyor. No credible evidence, oral or otherwise,
was  brought  on  record  about  any  lightning  strike.  The
irrefutable fact remains that the construction was faulty and
those defects were squarely responsible for the collapse of
the building. Significantly, no evidence was adduced of any
other building nearby suffering similar damage due to the
torrential rains and thunder on that day.
14. The appeal is, accordingly, allowed setting aside the order
dated 04.01.2023 and dismissing Consumer Case No.54 of 2014.
Registry shall return to the appellant the suitor’s fund
amount of 50,000/- along with the interest accrued thereon,₹
if any, under proper acknowledgement as per due procedure. 
15. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.
.....................J.
(SANJAY KUMAR)
.....................J.
(SANJEEV SACHDEVA)
NEW DELHI;
SEPTEMBER 22, 2026.

Application  (IA  NO.199259  OF  2026)  seeking
impleadment of the Ministry of Women and Child Development,
is allowed.
The  said  impleading  applicant  is  arrayed  as
respondent No.5.
Petitioner’s counsel to file amended memo of parties.
Learned Additional Solicitor General appearing for
the fifth respondent submitted that counter affidavit is
being filed in the office today. 
The same shall be taken on record.
We  have  heard  learned  senior  counsel  for  the
petitioner in the Writ Petition and the Special Leave
Petition respectively and also learned Additional Solicitor
General appearing for the respondent(s)-Union of India nad
learned counsel for the Bar Council of India.
We have perused the Gender Sensitisation and Sexual
Harassment  of  Women  at  the  Supreme  Court  of  India
(Prevention, Prohitbition and redressal) Regulations, 2013.
These Regulations have been made in respect of the Supreme
Court of India precincts only. 
In  order  to  have  a  wider  coverage  of  these
Regulations insofar as the High Courts and all Courts under
2

--- Page 196 ---
the District Judiciary as well as Tribunals of the Central
and State Governments, other quasi judicial authorities
etc, it is necessary that a separate set of Regulations are
made  as  we  find  that  the  provisions  of  the  Sexual
Harassment  of  the  Women  at  Workplace  (Prevention,
Prohitbition and redressal) Regulations, 2013 cannot be
applied in a straitjacket manner to an aggrieved women, who
belonged to the legal professions practising before other
Courts, Tribunals or other fora.
In the circumstances, we request the learned counsel
appearing for the respective parties to have a joint
consultation so as to draft a set of Regulations applicable
to all the aforesaid judicial and quasi-judicial Courts,
Tribunals and authorities.
Learned counsel for the respondent(s)-Bar Council
also submitted that she would seek instructions in the
matter and endeavour to bring about common Regulation
applicable to all the aggrieved women, who are in legal
profession.
We also request the learned counsel for the Bar
Council of India to ascertain from the Bar Councils of the
States as to whether any extant Regulations are being
implemented in this regard.
List this matter on 25.11.2026.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.4438 OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) NO.17837 OF 2026)
(@ DIARY NO.48480/2026) 
KUMAR @ UTHIRAKUMAR                                APPELLANT(S)
                                VERSUS
STATE, REP. BY INSPECTOR OF POLICE, TAMIL NADU     RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
Heard Ms. Shalini Kaul, learned counsel for the
appellant and Mr.B.Karunakaran, learned counsel for the
respondent-State of Tamil Nadu.
2. Delay condoned.
3. Leave granted.
4. The present appeal is directed against the order
dated 23.04.2019 passed by the High Court of judicature
at Madras in Criminal Appeal No.526/2018, by which the
conviction and sentence awarded to the appellant, vide
order dated 30.07.2018 passed by the Sessions Judge,
Mahila Court, Cuddalore in Sessions Case No.26/2017,
stood upheld. The appellant was accused in Crime No.
12/2016 registered for the commission of offence under
Sections 451, 376(i), 506(ii) of the Indian Penal Code,
1

--- Page 201 ---
1860 (for short the ‘IPC’) and upon trial, he was
convicted & sentenced under section 376(i) of the IPC to
undergo Rigorous Imprisonment for fourteen years, with a
fine of Rs.l5,000/- (Rupees Fifteen Thousand) and in
default  of  payment  of  fine,  to  undergo  Simple
Imprisonment for a period of two years; Under Section
451 of the IPC to undergo Rigorous Imprisonment for two
years with a fine of Rs.5,000/- (Rupees Five Thousand)
and in default of payment of fine to undergo Simple
Imprisonment  for  a  period  of  six  months  and  under
Section  506(ii)  of  the  IPC  to  undergo  Simple
Imprisonment for six months, with a fine of Rs.3,000/-
(Rupees Three Thousand) and in default of payment of
fine, to undergo Simple Imprisonment for a period of two
months,  stipulating  that  all  the  sentences  to  run
concurrently. 
5. Learned counsel for the appellant submitted that the
story in the FIR is different from the version in the
chargesheet submitted against the appellant and during
trial, there is further improvement in the statement of
witnesses. Certain discrepancies, which according to the
learned counsel were of such nature, which entitles the
appellant to get benefit of doubt in the facts and
circumstances of the present case.
6. Learned  counsel  for  the  respondent-State  submits
2

--- Page 202 ---
that the Trial Court has considered all such submissions
and dealt with the evidence recorded in detail, which
cannot be faulted and thus, according to him, the order
impugned needs no interference.
7. We have considered the matter in depth. Though,
there may be some force in the submission of learned
counsel for the appellant that there has been some sort
of  inconsistencies  with  regard  to  the  manner  and
presence of the so called witnesses and the FIR till the
time of recording of the evidence of those witnesses,
but ultimately, the reasoning given and the picture
which emerges is that the same cannot be brushed aside
as being unreliable. 
8. Furthermore, we find that even if the Court gives
some weightage to such discrepancies, only a case for
interference in the sentence would be made out and it
would not result in giving benefit of doubt based on
which acquittal can be recorded against the appellant.
9. Accordingly,  the  Court  finds  that  the  ends  of
justice, in the facts and circumstances of the present
case, would be served by reducing the sentence of 14
years rigorous imprisonment imposed upon the appellant
to 10 years of rigorous imprisonment, while maintaining
the fine.
10. Accordingly, the appeal is partially allowed to the
3

--- Page 203 ---
extent  that  while  upholding  the  conviction  of  the
appellant, the sentence is modified to 10 years rigorous
imprisonment.
11. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.
.....................J.
(AHSANUDDIN AMANULLAH)
....................J.
(MANMOHAN)
NEW DELHI
SEPTEMBER 18, 2026

--- Page 211 ---
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Heard Mr. Shailesh Madiyal, learned senior counsel
appearing for the petitioner and Mr. Nishanth Patil,
learned Additional Advocate General appearing for the
respondent-State.
2. The issue pertains to a recruitment Notification of
2nd April, 2012 inviting applications for the post of
Secondary  School  Assistant  Teacher  Grade-II.   The
petitioner applied under ‘Rural Candidates’ quota.  The
question is whether the petitioner was entitled to the
‘Rural Candidates’ quota.  To be eligible under the
‘Rural Candidates’ quota, the petitioner had to be of a
non-creamy layer category.  The petitioner contends that
a  certificate  of  31 st October,  2006  certifying  the
petitioner is a non creamy layer, would be admissible for
selection under the Notification of 2 nd April, 2012.
While the Tribunal agreed with the contention of the
petitioner on the ground that there was no prescription
of time limit, the High Court has set aside the order of
the Tribunal, rejecting the petitioner’s claim by holding
as under:
“13. In the instant case, the creamy layer
certificate produced by the applicant is placed
on record as Annexure-A6.  The said certificate
2

--- Page 212 ---
is dated 31.10.2006.  The said certificate is
more than five years prior to the last date for
submission of application, i.e.,10.05.2012.  The
said creamy layer certificate has expired in view
of the time prescribed under the 1992 Rules which
is  extracted  above.   Hence,  the  selecting
authority or appointing authority could not have
given any credence to the said creamy layer
certificate dated 31.10.2006.  The creamy layer
certificate dated 31.10.2013 produced along with
the  representation  is  a  certificate  obtained
subsequent  to  preparation  of  the  additional
select list i.e. more than one and half year
after last date for submission of application and
the same cannot be taken note of for selection,
since it is not within the last date prescribed
under the notification inviting application.  The
clause  26  –  General  Instructions  requires  a
candidate to obtain the certificates with regard
to reservation and other benefits, prior to the
last date for submitting the application and to
produce the same for verification when called
for.  It also makes it clear that failing to
produce such certificate, the candidate would not
be entitled to reservation.  The purpose behind
the condition to obtain certificates prior to the
last  date  for  submitting  application  is  to
determine eligibility as on the last date for
submitting application.  It is settled position
of law that the eligibility in all respects in a
recruitment process shall have to be determined
as on the last date for submitting application.
3

--- Page 213 ---
The other reason for such condition is that
income would vary from year to year depending on
the avocation carried on by each person.  Thus,
both the certificates produced by the petitioner
cannot be looked into and as such the selecting /
appointing authority has rightly rejected those
certificates.
14. We have gone through the impugned order
passed by the Tribunal.  The Tribunal proceeded
to allow the application relying upon clause-19
of the notification inviting application and the
Tribunal failed to notice clause-16 as well as
clause-26  of  the  notification  inviting
application wherein it is made clear that a
candidate  is  required  to  obtain  certificate
regarding reservation and certificate regarding
any other benefit prior to the last date for
submitting the application.  The Tribunal failed
to take note of the provisions of 1990 Act as
well as 1992 Rules.  The order passed by the
Tribunal is wholly erroneous and is the result of
failure  to  notice  the  general  conditions  or
instructions  contained  in  the  notification
inviting applications.”
3. We noticed that the advertisement is of the year
2012.  Much water has flown, since 14 years have elapsed.
The selections, according to the learned counsel for the
respondent, are long concluded.  At this distance of
time, no purpose would be served by addressing this issue
4

--- Page 214 ---
in  this  matter.   Hence,  while  not  exercising  our
jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution of
India, we leave the question of law, if any, open for
consideration in an appropriate case.
4. The Special Leave Petition is dismissed in the
above terms.
5. Pending applications shall stand disposed of.
(ANITA MALHOTRA)                          (MANOJ KUMAR)
     DEPUTY REGISTRAR                          COURT MASTER

were  filed  before  the  NCDRC  (Revision  Petition
No.598/2021 filed by the appellant herein), only the
revision petition filed by the appellant herein was
dismissed whereas the Revision Petition Nos. 375 and 450
of 2021 filed by the other respondents are pending
consideration before the NCDRC.
4. Learned counsel for the appellant submitted that the
appellant could not have been singled out whereas the
other revision petitions are pending consideration. This
may also lead to contradictory orders being passed by
the NCDRC.  In the circumstances, this Court may set
aside the impugned order and remand the matter to the
NCDRC so that Revision Petition No.598/2021 filed by the
appellant herein could be clubbed with the aforesaid two
revision petitions and the same could be heard and
disposed of by a common judgment and order.
5. Learned counsel for respondent No.1 who was the
complainant  before  the  District  Forum  vehemently
contended that in view of the impugned order being
passed by the NCDRC all that remains is for the NCDRC to
follow the said order and dismiss the other two revision
petitions also.  Therefore, it is unnecessary for this
case to be remanded to the NCDRC.
6.  However, learned senior counsel and learned counsel
appearing for the other respondents also pointed out
that they have their respective contentions to urge
before the NCDRC and they have good case on merits and
2

--- Page 237 ---
hence the impugned order may not be an impediment for
the  NCDRC  in  the  consideration  of  their  revision
petitions.
7.  Having heard learned senior counsel and learned
counsel appearing for the respective parties, we find
that the ends of justice would be met in the instant
case, if we set aside the impugned judgment of the NCDRC
passed in Revision Petition No.598/2021 and remand this
case  to the NCDRC with a direction to the NCDRC to  tag
this matter with Revision Petition Nos.375 and 450 of
2021  and  to  hear  the  arguments  on  behalf  of  the
respective parties and dispose the same by a common
judgment and order. We say so for the salient reason
that in respect of the same cause of action other
matters pending before the NCDRC could not have been
heard independently.  This may lead to contradictory
judgments and orders being passed.
8.  In the circumstances, we set aside the impugned
order, remand the matter and restore Revision Petition
No.598/2021 on the file of the NCDRC and direct that
Revision Petition No.598/2021 be tagged with Revision
Petition Nos. 375 and 450 of 2021 so as to be heard
together and disposed of by a common judgment and order.
9. Since the complaint was filed by respondent No.1 in
the year 2013, we request the NCDRC to dispose of the
Revision Petitions as expeditiously as possible.
10. Since the parties before this Court are represented
3

--- Page 238 ---
by  their  respective  senior  counsel  and  counsel,  we
direct them to appear before the NCDRC  on 26.10.2026
without expecting any separate notices from the said
Commission.  
 The appeal is allowed and disposed of in the  
aforesaid terms.

CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO(S).          OF 2026

SUKANTI DEVI                                    APPELLANT
VERSUS
THE STATE OF BIHAR                             RESPONDENT
O R D E R
Leave granted.
This  appeal  challenges  the  order  dated
26.08.2022 passed by the High Court of Judicature
at Patna in Criminal Miscellaneous Application
No. 19612 of 2022.
Apprehending arrest in connection with crime
registered pursuant to FIR No.397 of 2021 lodged
with  Chiraiya  Police  Station,  East  Champaran
District in respect of the offence punishable
under Sections 272 and 273 of IPC and under
Section 30(a) of the Bihar Prohibition and Excise
Act, 2016, the appellant preferred an application
before the High Court seeking anticipatory bail
in terms of Section 438 of the Code of Criminal
Procedure, 1973 [in short, “the Code”]
1

--- Page 241 ---
Said application for anticipatory bail has
been rejected by the High Court vide the impugned
order dated 26.08.2022 Hence, instant appeal has
been preferred.
By  order  dated  11.06.2026,  while  issuing
notice, this Court granted interim protection in
favour of the appellant.
We  have  heard  learned  counsel  for  the
appellant in support of the appeal and learned
counsel for the respondent-State.
Learned counsel for the appellant submitted
that merely because 30 litres of country made
liquor was recovered from the appellant’s house,
FIR No.397 of 2021 dated 29.12.2021 has been
foisted on her; that the appellant has been
cooperating  with  the  investigation.  In  the
circumstances, the interim order may be made
absolute by allowing this appeal and setting
aside the impugned order.
Per  contra ,  learned  counsel  for  the
respondent-State with reference to the counter
affidavit contended that there is no merit in
2

--- Page 242 ---
this appeal and it is also not known as to
whether the appellant has been cooperating with
the investigation or not. Hence, this appeal may
be dismissed.
Considering the circumstances on record, in
our view, the appellant is entitled to the relief
claimed under Section 438 of the Code.
We, therefore, allow this appeal and set
aside the order passed by the High Court dated
26.08.2022. 
We direct that in the event of arrest of the
appellant, the Arresting Officer shall release
the appellant on bail subject to furnishing cash
security  in  the  sum  of  Rs.25,000/-  (Rupees
Twenty-Five  Thousand  only)  with  two  like
sureties.
It  is  directed  that  the  appellant  shall
extend  complete  cooperation  in  the  ensuing
investigation. 
The appellant shall not misuse her liberty
and shall not in any way influence the witnesses
or tamper with the material on record.
3

--- Page 243 ---
With the aforesaid directions, the criminal
appeal is allowed.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Pursuant to our order dated 12.08.2026, the Committee has
prepared the ‘Yamuna Action Plan’ and the same has been

--- Page 247 ---
submitted for our perusal.
2. In the status note appended to the letter which forwarded
the action plan to the Amicus,  it is mentioned that the
‘Yamuna Action Plan’ does not have any proposal for removal
or relocation of encroachments/unauthorized structures on
the riverbeds, floodplains or drains falling within the
National Capital Territory of Delhi.
3. At page 112 of the Action Plan, it is mentioned that 1799
unauthorized  colonies  have  been  identified  for  which
integrated sewerage system is being developed and the work
to the extent of 73% is complete. Rest is at various stages
of implementation.
4. We notice that in the Master Plan for Delhi-2047, a special
initiative  for  rejuvenation  of  river  Yamuna  and  its
floodplains is envisaged. However, what is striking is that
it  dichotomizes  floodplains  by  earmarking  active
floodplains.  On  what  basis  floodplains  have  been
differentiated by treating some as active needs to be
explained.
5. Further,  how  many  unauthorized  colonies  identified  are
located over the floodplains must be disclosed so that we
can assess whether the action plan is one which would be
effective in serving the avowed purpose. 
6. Additionally, to have a clear understanding of the action
plan and the requisite steps proposed thereunder, we would
require a representative from the Ministry of Home Affairs
to make a Power Point Presentation on the action plan and
the various steps envisaged thereunder. Learned Amicus has
suggested that it can be arranged on 07.10.2026 at 4.00 pm.
We accept the suggestion. Let necessary arrangements be
made for the same on 07.10.2026 at 4.00 pm.    

--- Page 248 ---
7. Besides, we would like clarity on the issue as to whether
the Master Plan for Delhi-2047 is in sync with the ‘Yamuna
Action Plan’ which has been placed before us.

--- Page 249 ---
8. List on 4.11.2026.  By the next date, a report/affidavit may
be filed dealing with the aspects highlighted above. The
Amicus Curiae is permitted to convey this order to the
concerned Ministry.

      UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the 
following
                             O R D E R
IA No.239572/2026 in CRL. A. NOS.1277-1280/2024:
1. This application  has been filed  by accused No.3
(Abdul Nabi @ Chand Pasha) for grant of bail by suspending
the sentence imposed on him.
2. The applicant – accused No.3 (Abdul Nabi @ Chand
Pasha) came to be tried alongwith other accused for an
offence punishable under Sections 143, 148, 302, 201 and
114 read with Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860
(“IPC”) in Sessions Case No.216/2012 and acquitted on
23.09.2016  for  the  said  offences  on  appreciation  of
evidence. The appellate court reversed the said finding and
convicted accused Nos.1 to 4 under Section 302 read with
34 of the IPC, accused Nos.5 and 6 under Section 302 read
with Sections 114 and 34 of the IPC and accused Nos.1, 2
and 4 under Section 201 of the IPC. The acquittal under
Sections 143 and 148 of the IPC was maintained. The trial
2

--- Page 252 ---
court by its judgment of acquittal had opined that the
evidence  of  eye-witnesses  PW-2,  PW-3  and  PW-4  was
unreliable  and  the  prosecution  had  failed  to  prove
satisfactorily the motive and recovery of weapons. The
deficiencies in the eye-witnesses’ statements also swayed
in the mind of the trial court to acquit them. The High Court
by  the  impugned  judgment  after  re-appreciation  of
evidence  was  of  the  view  that  the  eye-witnesses’
statements would establish their presence at the scene of
crime and they had also identified the accused. The fact
that there was no Test Identification Parade conducted
seems  to  have  not  been  taken  into  account  by  the
appellate court.
3. Learned  counsel  appearing  for  the  State  would
oppose the grant of bail by contending that applicant had
sought for grant of bail on earlier occasion and this Court
by order dated 22.08.2024 had rejected the same and the
prayer  of  accused  No.2  (Yogeesha)  had  never  been
considered by this Court and as such the applicant cannot
claim parity. 
3

--- Page 253 ---
4. A perusal of the order dated 22.08.2024 would
indicate that prayer of the present applicant was not
entertained by opining that it was not a case for grant of
suspension of sentence and bail ‘at that stage’. This Court
having taken note of the fact that there was a reversal of
acquittal passed by the trial court into a conviction by the
High Court and the fact that actual motive for the incident
requires to be examined in the light of divergent views
expressed by the Courts, we are of the considered view
that sentence imposed on the appellant / applicant (Abdul
Nabi @ Chand Pasha – A-3) deserves to be suspended and
he should be released on bail. Accordingly, the application
is allowed. The sentence imposed on the applicant –
accused  No.3  (Abdul  Nabi  @  Chand  Pasha)  stands
suspended and applicant – accused No.3 (Abdul Nabi @
Chand Pasha) is ordered to be enlarged on bail by the
jurisdictional Sessions Court on such terms and conditions
as it deems fit to impose. 
5. It is needless to state that the observations made
hereinabove is confined only for the limited purpose of
4

--- Page 254 ---
examining the prayer for suspension of sentence and
grant of bail and it shall in no way affect the final
adjudication. 
  (NEHA GUPTA)                      (AVGV RAMU)
COURT MASTER (SH)               COURT MASTER (NSH)

2. The  present  petition  calls  in  question  the
correctness of the order dated 16 th April, 2025 passed by
the High Court of Judicature for Rajasthan at Jaipur in
S.B.Criminal Misc. Suspension of Sentence Application No.
1326 of 2023 in S.B.Criminal Appeal No.2129 of 2023.  By
the said order, the application of the petitioner for
suspension of sentence and to enlarge the petitioner on
bail has been declined. The petitioner has been convicted
under Sections 376(AB) of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 and
Section 5(M)/6 of  Protection of Children from Sexual
Offences Act, 2012 and further sentenced to undergo
rigorous  imprisonment  for  20  years  and  a  fine  of
Rs.50,000/-.
3. When the matter was listed before this Court on 18 th
August, 2026, the following order was passed:
“1.  Application  for  exemption  from  filing
official translation is allowed. 
2.  Heard  Mr.  Namit  Saxena,  learned  counsel
appearing for the petitioner and Mr. Divyank
Panwar, learned counsel appearing, on advance
notice, for the respondent-State. 
3. Issue notice.
4. Learned counsel for the petitioner seeks
time to file additional documents primarily to
establish that the chain of custody of the
samples  sent  for  DNA  examination  was  not
complete. Additional documents be filed on or
before the next date of hearing.
         SLP (Criminal) No.13380 of 2026                                                                Page 2 of 4

--- Page 279 ---
5. List the matter on 2nd September, 2026.
6.  In  the  meantime,  a  short  counter
affidavit/status  report  be  filed  by  the
respondent-State.
4. Today, during the course of hearing, apart from
referring to the evidence of the victim as well as her
father, learned counsel for the petitioner also referred
to the application filed by him placing the alleged
discrepancy in the chain of custody of the samples sent
for DNA examination.
5. Learned counsel also submits that the petitioner
was a juvenile at the time of the alleged incident and is
presently lodged in the rehabilitation home.
6. Learned counsel for the respondent-State vehemently
opposes the suspension of sentence.
7. Having  considered  the  overall  facts  and
circumstances, we are inclined to suspend the sentence of
the petitioner and enlarge him on bail, pending hearing
of the Criminal Appeal No.2129 of 2023 before the High
Court.
8. The sentence imposed on the petitioner is suspended
and the petitioner is directed to be enlarged on bail
subject to the satisfaction of the Trial Court, pending
disposal of the Criminal Appeal by the High Court.
         SLP (Criminal) No.13380 of 2026                                                                Page 3 of 4

above terms.
10. Pending application shall also stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Criminal Appeal No.4508 of 2026
(Arising out of SLP (Crl.) No.3916 of 2026)
P S Khengar and Anr.               ...Appellant (s)
Versus
Sanjeev Paliwal and Anr.       ...Respondent (s)
 
O R D E R
Leave granted.
2. The appellants are respectively the Chief Municipal Officer and
the Revenue Inspector of the Municipal Council, Sironj, District
Vidisha. The criminal prosecution with which they are concerned,
arose from a site inspection conducted for preparing a  panchnama
for due measurement and demarcation of a property. The 1 st
respondent is the owner of a residential building, Hanuman Marg,
Ward No.11, Sironj, District Vidisha, against which building, a notice
was issued directing demolition, for reason of the dilapidated
condition of the same. On the 1 st respondent attempting to demolish
the building, his brother is said to have created obstruction, and this
resulted in the 1st respondent making a request to the Chief Municipal
Officer to determine the area, boundaries and demarcation of the
property.
3. It is the case of the 1 st respondent who registered the
complaint under Section 156(3) of Code of Criminal Procedure, 19731,
1  In short ‘CrPC’

--- Page 298 ---
that though a panchnama  was prepared, on seeking a copy, it was
informed that the same was destroyed by the 2 nd appellant, on
instructions of the 1 st appellant. The Judicial Magistrate First Class,
Sironj, District Vidisha, before whom the complaint was registered,
rejected it for reason of no sanction having been obtained under
Section 197 CrPC. 
4. The learned Additional Sessions Judge, Sironj, District Vidisha,
however allowed a criminal revision filed holding that destroying a
panchnama  prepared cannot be treated as an act done in discharge
of the official duties and, therefore, there is no reason to find the
requirement of a sanction. The High Court concurred with the
Additional Sessions Judge and hence, the appellants are before this
Court challenging the order of the High Court.
5. Without going into the question of sanction, we looked at the
specific reply, based on which the allegation has been raised, which
is produced as Annexure P4. In Paragraph 3 of Annexure P4, the
appellants admit that there was an inspection conducted of the
property and there was an attempt to carry out the measurement
and prepare a panchnama. However, a dispute arose between the
brothers, leading to a fight on the spot itself, due to which
panchnama  proceedings could not be completed. Though separate
panchnamas were being prepared, since dispute and fight ensued, no

--- Page 299 ---
preparation of panchnama was carried out.
6. We find absolutely no reason to permit the continuance of the
proceedings before the Judicial Magistrate First Class, Sironj, District
Vidisha, who has issued summons, as indicated from Annexure P10,
after the revision was allowed. 
7. We allow the appeal, setting aside the impugned order of the
High Court and Annexure P8-order of the Additional Sessions Judge,
Sironj, District Vidisha. The complaint filed under Section 156(3),
produced at Annexure P5, shall stand quashed and no further
proceeding shall be taken on that count.
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand rejected.

                (J. B. PARDIWALA)
....……….……………………. J.

2.  Without adverting to the merits, learned counsel for the
applicant/appellant no.3 submits that two of the co-accused,
who have been convicted in the case, had been granted the
privilege of suspension of sentence and release on the ground
that they had suffered nine years of actual incarceration. In
the  present  case,  it  was  pointed  out  that  the
applicant/appellant no.3-Hola Ghosh is similarly situated to

--- Page 303 ---
3
the co-accused namely, appellant no.1-Dilu Ghosh and appellant
no.4-Badan  @  Swarup  Ghosh.  It  was  submitted  that  the
applicant/appellant no.3-Hola Ghosh has suffered more than
nine years of actual incarceration and thus, on the ground of
parity, his case may be considered.
3.  Learned Advocate-on-Record for the respondent-State of
West Bengal submits that the co-accused/appellant no.1-Dilu
Ghosh’s case can be differentiated on the ground that he was
only  present  at  the  place  of  occurrence  whereas,  the
applicant/appellant no.3-Hola Ghosh was one of the persons,
who had actually taken active part in the crime by chopping
the hands of the dead body. However, it was not controverted
that the co-accused/appellant no.4-Badan @ Swarup Ghosh is
similarly situated.
4.  Having considered the matter, we are of the considered
opinion that in view the co-accused/appellant no.4-Badan @
Swarup  Ghosh,  being  similarly  situated  to  the
applicant/appellant no.3-Hola Ghosh, the prayer for suspension
of sentence and grant of bail to the applicant/appellant no.3-
Hola Ghosh is fit to be allowed. Accordingly, t he sentence of

the High Court in a writ appeal.  The Division Bench, vide
impugned order dated 20 th July, 2026 passed in W.A. (MD)
No.982 OF 2026, dismissed the writ appeal.  Relevant
paragraph 7 of the impugned order, is reproduced as under: 
“7. In such circumstances, we are inclined
to exercise our jurisdiction to set aside
even  that  portion  of  the  order  of  the
learned  Single  Judge  by  which  the  writ
petition was partly allowed, though the said
2

--- Page 311 ---
portion is not the subject matter of the
present appeal.  Accordingly, the order of
the learned Single Judge is set aside, in
its entirety, and the writ petition stands
dismissed in    toto  . Consequently, the writ  
appeal  stands  dismissed.  No  costs.
Consequently,  connected  miscellaneous
petition is closed.”
7. The net result is that the petitioner was rendered
worse off in its own appeal inasmuch as even that portion
of the order of the learned Single Judge remanding back to
the employer, was set aside. Aggrieved, the petitioner is
before us. 
8. During the pendency of the writ appeal, on 20 th May,
2026 read with 17th July, 2026, a speaking order was passed
by the respondent-Corporation upholding the forfeiture and
blacklisting.
9. In this scenario, we are of the opinion that the
petitioner should be granted liberty to challenge the
subsequent orders dated 20 th May, 2026 and 17 th July, 2026
by way of a fresh writ petition. 
10. Mr. Purushottam Sharma Tripathi, learned counsel for
the respondent-Corporation submits that the respondent-
Corporation will not raise any objection with regard to the
petitioner approaching the grievance redressal committee.
We place this statement on record. 
11. In case any writ petition is filed challenging the
3

subsequent orders, the same shall be decided on its own

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.                OF 2026
(@SLP(CRL.) NO.13903 OF 2026)
SUDHIR KUMAR ..... APPELLANT(S)
              VERSUS
STATE OF BIHAR ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Heard.
2. Leave granted.
3. The appellant was working as a District Agriculture Officer-cum-Project
Director and the complainant was working as a Block Technical Manager.
Initially, one Smt.Pramila Devi made a complaint seeking investigation as to
how  the  funds  sanctioned  for  disbursement  to  farmers  had  been
misappropriated. An FIR was lodged against the complainant and an enquiry
began against him and the complainant was suspended from service.
4. The complainant made a request to rejoin to his post. To accept the
request of the complainant, the appellant is said to have demanded a bribe
of Rs.2 Lakhs and under compulsion the complainant is said to have paid
Rs.1,50,000/- and Rs.31,000/- in two installments for his joining. The
remaining  amount  of  Rs.19,000/-was  left  unpaid  and the  appellant
1                                                                                            SLP(CRL.) NO.13903 OF 2026

--- Page 318 ---
demanded payment of the said amount. Hence, the complainant lodged a
complaint before the police and after verification, police accompanied the
complainant to appellant’s house where conversation of the bribe amount
between them was also recorded. A trap was laid on 03.01.2026 and at
around 08:40 am the police along with the complainant reached the
residence of the accused/appellant and complainant has stated that accused
had demanded the balance Rs.19,000/- and on payment of same it was
counted by the appellant and notes were kept in his trousers namely left
side pocket. The tainted notes are said to have been recovered from the left
pocket of the trousers of the appellant and hand of the appellants were
dipped in Sodium Carbonate solution, which turned pink. Hence, appellant
was arrested and he has been in custody from last eight months.
Investigation having been concluded, chargesheet has been filed.
5.  Having heard the learned counsels appearing for the parties and after
noticing that it is a case of trap and appellant was caught red-handed, at
this stage, we do not propose to enter into the merits. Suffice it to state that
the appellant has been in judicial custody from 03.01.2026 and chargesheet
has been filed, the custodial interrogation, even if any, would not be
warranted. The appellant is said to be aged about 62 years and is said to be
suffering from age related diseases and there being no other allegation, we
are of the considered view that there is no flight risk. Hence appellant is
entitled for relief of bail.
6. Hence, the appeal is allowed. Impugned order is set aside. Appellant is
ordered to be released on bail by the jurisdictional court on such terms and
conditions as it may deem fit.
2                                                                                            SLP(CRL.) NO.13903 OF 2026

--- Page 319 ---

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.                OF 2026
(@SLP(CRL.) NO.13234 OF 2026)
RAKSHAK @ RAKSHAKUMAR ..... APPELLANT(S)
              VERSUS
STATE OF KARNATAKA ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Heard.
2. Leave granted.
3. Appellant has been arraigned as an accused in FIR No.127/2025
registered at Chadachan Police Station, Vijayapura for the offences
punishable under Sections 309, 351(2), 127(1) of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita,
2023 (BNS) and Sections 25 and 27 of the Arms Act, 1959.
4.  It is the case of the prosecution that on 16.09.2025, approximately
between 06:30 pm to 07:20 pm the Accused Nos.1 to 5 committed
robbery/dacoity in State Bank of India, Chadachan Branch and the
appellant(A6) had helped A1 to secure a country made pistol. It is also the
allegation against him that he along with A1 to A7 committed the robbery.
However, it is the contention of learned counsel appearing for the
appellant that he never entered the State of Karnataka and was arrested
1                                                                                                    SLP(CRL.) NO.13234 OF 2026

--- Page 322 ---
from his native place Samastipur, Bihar. Hence, contenting that he has
been falsely implicated that too based on co-accused statement, he seeks
for being enlarged on bail.
5. Having heard the learned counsels appearing for the parties, we notice
that appellant was not named in the FIR and no incriminating material has
been recovered from his person or from his premises. The prosecution
case rests on the statement made by the co-accused. As to whether the
appellant had received the consideration as alleged by the prosecution for
sale of the firearm to A1, will have to be examined after evaluating the
entire evidence that may be tendered.
6. At this stage, it cannot be said that the continued incarceration of the
appellant  is  warranted.  Though  the learned  counsel  appearing  for
respondent-State would vehemently contend that appellant being a
resident of Bihar and he is likely to abscond and thereby the progress of
the trial would be tardy pray for rejection of the bail, we are not inclined to
accept the same.
7. Having regard to the allegations made against the appellant, we are of
the considered view that appellant is entitled for being released on bail. It
would suffice to allay the apprehension of the prosecution by imposing the
following conditions on the appellant apart from the conditions that may
be imposed by the jurisdictional trial Court.
(i) the appellant shall mark his attendance every fortnight in
Samastipur Police Station, Bihar, till conclusion of the trial;
2                                                                                                    SLP(CRL.) NO.13234 OF 2026

--- Page 323 ---
(ii) the appellant shall furnish his mobile number and also the
residential address of his native place to the jurisdictional
Sessions Court.
8. Accordingly, appeal is allowed. Impugned order is set aside. Appellant is
ordered to be released on bail.  Apart from the aforestated two (2)
conditions the jurisdictional court would be at liberty to impose such other
and further conditions as it deems fit.

..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
 
1. Leave granted. 
2. The appellant, K.K. Rajagopal, is aggrieved by the order dated
09.06.2025 passed by the High Court of Judicature at Madras in
Criminal R.C. No. 274/2023, confirming the conviction and
sentence imposed upon him by the learned Judicial Magistrate,
Court No. 1, Salem, vide judgment dated 25.02.2020 passed in
C.C. No. 449/2005, for the offences punishable under Sections
468 and 120(b) of the Indian Penal Code, 1860. 
3. The case against the appellant, a Duty Doctor in Kamala
Hospital, was that he had altered the entry made in the
accident register maintained at the hospital, by modifying the
time of the accident as 07.30 p.m. in the place of 02.30 p.m.
4. We find from the record that the accident register, which was
allegedly modified by the appellant, was never produced in
evidence. 
1

--- Page 338 ---
5. Reliance was placed by the trial court upon the investigation
report  said  to  have  been  submitted  by  the  investigator
appointed by the Insurance Company, wherein he had recorded to
the effect that the appellant had made such a modification. In
the absence of the primary evidence,  viz., the accident
register, which the appellant allegedly modified, the trial
court was not justified in returning a finding of guilt
against him and sentencing him to imprisonment for a period of
six months. 
6. The High Court was equally in error in overlooking this
crucial aspect and in confirming the conviction and sentence
imposed upon the appellant.
7. We may also note that, by order dated 04.08.2025, this Court
granted exemption from surrendering to the appellant and while
issuing notice on 14.08.2025, the said order was extended. 
8. The  appeal  is,  accordingly,  allowed,  setting  aside  the
judgment  dated  25.02.2020  in  C.C.  No.  449/2005  and  the
confirmation thereof by the impugned order passed by the High
Court in Crl. R.C. No. 274/2023. 
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.       OF 2026
(arising out of SLP(Crl.) No. 5954/2026)
BALDEV SINGH ..... APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
CBI ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted. 
2. The appellant, Baldev Singh, was convicted by the learned
Special Judge, Tis Hazari Courts, Delhi, under Sections 7 and
13(2)  read  with  Section  13(1)(d)  of  the  Prevention  of
Corruption Act, 1988 1,  and was sentenced to two and a half
years imprisonment with fine of 10,000/- (Rupees ten thousand₹
only) in relation to his conviction under Section 7 of the
P.C. Act and to imprisonment for a period of one and a half
years coupled with fine of 5,000/- (Rupees five thousand₹
only) for his conviction under Section 13(2) read with Section
13(1)(d) of the P.C. Act. Default sentences for non-payment of
fine were also indicated. 
3. Aggrieved thereby, the appellant, Baldev Singh, filed Criminal
Appeal No. 567/2001 before the High Court of Delhi. By
judgment dated 28.01.2026 passed therein, a learned Judge of
the High Court dismissed his appeal. Aggrieved thereby, the
1For short ‘PC Act’
1

--- Page 346 ---
appellant is before this Court. 
4. We are informed that the age of the appellant, Baldev Singh,
as on date, is over 70 years. The incident, in relation to
which he was convicted of the aforestated offences, dates back
to 08.11.1995. 
5. Having heard the learned counsel for the parties and upon
perusing the record, we find that sufficient incriminating
circumstances were clearly made out to support the conclusion
drawn by the trial court against the appellant that he was
guilty of the offences charged. 
6. We are conscious of the fact that the appellant, Baldev Singh,
suffered incarceration as an under-trial only for a period of
five days in November, 1995, but he has been in prison since
13.02.2026, after the dismissal of his appeal by the High
Court. 
7. Given  the  length  of  time  that  has  elapsed  since  his
conviction, it would be a travesty of justice to sustain the
long sentence of imprisonment that he would have to the suffer
at this stage owing to the dismissal of his appeal by the High
Court. 
8. We may note that the minimum sentence prescribed for an
offence under Section 7 of the P.C. Act, as applicable at the
relevant time, entailed imprisonment for not less than six
months. Similarly, the minimum sentence of imprisonment for an
offence under Section 13(2) of the P.C. Act, at that time, was
one year. 
2

--- Page 347 ---
9. As already noted, the appellant was incarcerated on 13.02.2026
and has been in prison since then. He has, therefore, suffered
over 9 months of incarceration in all. Given the length of
time that has passed and his advanced age, we deem it
sufficient  in  the  interest  of  justice  to  exercise  our
jurisdiction under Article 142 of the Constitution and reduce
the sentence of imprisonment visited upon the appellant,
Baldev Singh, to the minimum sentences applicable at the
relevant point of time. 
10. The order of sentence dated 03.08.2001 passed by the learned
Special Judge, Tis Hazari Courts, Delhi, confirmed by the High
Court  of  Delhi  by  way  of  the  impugned  judgment  shall,
accordingly, stand modified and the sentences, which are to
run  concurrently,  shall  stand  reduced  to  one  year  of
imprisonment.  The  fine  amounts  shall,  however,  remain
unaltered and, in consequence, the default sentences in that
regard shall also remain unaltered. 
11.The appeal is, accordingly, allowed to the extent indicated
above.  
12.Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.  
.....................J.
(SANJAY KUMAR)
.....................J.
(SANJEEV SACHDEVA)
NEW DELHI;
SEPTEMBER 21, 2026.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL  NO(S).  421/2011
PUNJAB WAKF BOARD                                  APPELLANT(S)
                                VERSUS
DOABA COLLEGE & ANR.                               RESPONDENT(S)
 
O R D E R
1. The present appeal has been filed assailing the impugned
judgement dated 21.07.2010, passed by the High Court of
Punjab  and  Haryana,  wherein,  the  revision  petition
challenging the judgement of the Wakf Tribunal dated
30.05.2008 was dismissed. The appellant-Wakf Board had
filed  a  plaint  seeking  eviction  and  recovery  of
possession of suit property admeasuring 7 kanals and 14
marlas on the strength of a Gazette Notification dated
06.02.1971 and corrigendum dated 01.06.1991, issued by
the Central Government. The appellant further sought for

--- Page 362 ---
2
recovery of arrears of rent along with interest from the
defendant/respondents.  It  was  alleged  that  the  suit
property  was  leased  out  to  the  defendants  w.e.f
01.05.1967, on a monthly rent basis and the cause of
action arose when conditions of the lease were violated.
2. The Wakf Tribunal dismissed the suit, by rejecting the
contentions raised by the appellant, with respect to the
factum  of  ownership  of  the  appellant  or  that  the
defendants were its tenants. The High Court vide the
impugned  judgement  passed  in  Civil  Revision  No.
4232/2009, affirmed the findings of the Wakf Tribunal.
Aggrieved, the present appeal has been preferred.
3. We have heard the learned Senior counsel appearing for
the appellant and the learned Senior counsel appearing
for the respondents.
4. We have also perused the impugned judgment and the
records.
5. We are inclined to interfere with the impugned judgment,
by remitting the matter back to the High Court for fresh
consideration on a short ground, without going into the
other issue(s), as we find that the admission made by the
respondents/defendants  have  not  been  taken  into
consideration by the High Court.
6. In such view of the matter, the impugned order stands set

--- Page 363 ---
3
aside, leaving all the issues left open, including the
fact of so called admission made by the respondents
before us. 
7. Taking note of the long pendency of the proceedings, we
request the High Court to dispose of the pending revision
petition, within a period of six months from the date of
receipt of a copy of this order.  
8. The appeal stands allowed, accordingly.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

  [M.M. SUNDRESH]
       ………………………………………………………………………J.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL No.            /2026
[@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRL.) NO. 17801/2026]
VEER CHAND                                       Appellant(s)
VERSUS
STATE OF HIMACHAL PRADESH                       Respondent(s)
 O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. Heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. This appeal arises from an order dated 07.04.2026 passed
by the High Court of Himachal Pradesh rejecting the
regular bail prayer of the appellant in connection with
First Information Report No.65 of 2024, registered at
P.S. Nalagarh, District Solan, H.P.
4. The submission on behalf of the appellant is that there
is no incriminating recovery from the appellant, and his
complicity is based on confessional statement of co-
accused.  Besides, the prosecution relies on some money
transactions.  It has also been submitted that by now
the appellant has suffered incarceration of over one
year 9 months and in between co-accused Mahavir has been
admitted to bail under orders of this Court.
5. The learned counsel for the respondent-State has opposed
the prayer for bail but could not dispute that there is
Crl.A. @ SLP (Crl.) No. 17801/2026                             1

--- Page 370 ---
no recovery of the contraband from the appellant.  He
also could not dispute that Mahavir has been admitted to
bail under orders of this Court.
6. Having regard to the above, without expressing any
opinion on merits of the prosecution case, we are of the
view that the appellant is entitled to be released on
bail pending trial.
7. The appeal is, accordingly, allowed. The order passed by
the  High  Court  rejecting  the  bail  prayer  of  the
appellant is set aside.
8. The appellant shall be released on bail on such terms
and conditions as the trial court may deem fit to impose
in the facts and circumstances of the case.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.
